A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JOLA research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison across the revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, gating and component ablations, scaling experiments, and generated examples in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds component-selection, data-scaling, learning-rate and hyperparameter-sensitivity results.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 retains the same additive/multiplicative interventions, separate Hard-Concrete gates, expected-L0 objective and expected-gate inference procedure. The scalar, input-free gate explanation clarifies the existing method. Appendix A's conflicting per-input wording does not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight commonsense datasets, fourteen MMLU-Pro domains and four GEM generation tasks. The expanded sample-size experiments reuse SIQA and WinoGrande without introducing new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The main baseline set and SMP/DSP/PASS comparison remain unchanged. Comparator membership changes locally in the gate ablation: v1 Figure 5 includes zero-shot, whereas v3 Table 2 omits that reference and adds gated MLP and combined Attention+MLP variants.

E3.justification: v1 Appendix D.3 reports averaging five baseline configurations; v3 Appendix F.3 instead describes per-task grid search and validation-based selection of the best configuration. Section 4.3 still describes averaging, leaving the actual procedure unresolved, but the reported protocol changes substantially. Added experiments extend training sizes to 100,000 and compare four learning-rate schedules.

E4.justification: v3 expands the gate ablation to MLP and combined interventions, adds component-by-sample-size analysis in Figure 10, learning-rate comparisons in Table 8 and baseline hyperparameter sensitivity in Figure 11. It also extends data scaling beyond 1,000 examples and adds intermediate OBQA gate snapshots. These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Appendix A newly describes baseline variability as 'up to ±5% accuracy' across datasets, without defining the statistic or its estimation. This is a limited variability-reporting addition, not evidence of additional runs. The sampling seed remains 42, and neither version supplies repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the six detailed benchmark tables retain identical numerical results. However, v3 adds substantial scaling and sensitivity results, including LoRA overtaking JOLA at larger sample sizes and reported OBQA gate closure rates of 86% additive and 94% multiplicative. The gate-ablation results are revised, and Table 3 introduces separate trainable/active counts, including 0.0065%/0.0002% for JOLA.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix A adds an approximate trainable-parameter fraction formula, Equation 6, alongside the trainable/active distinction. The intervention equations, sparsity objective and learning-rate formula remain substantively unchanged. Appendix B largely restates existing intervention mathematics; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: joint localization and intervention learning, the effectiveness of attention-head editing, and strong low-resource performance across tasks and model sizes.

C2.justification: v3 materially expands the interpretation of applicability and efficiency: Section 6.5 acknowledges a gap behind LoRA at larger data sizes, Appendix A distinguishes training from active intervention parameters, and Appendix C attributes combined-component degradation to overfitting or representational interference despite additional data. These extend the earlier discussion beyond predominantly positive low-resource findings.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses baseline early stopping, clarifies that only the Hard-Concrete scale parameter is trained, and specifies rank 8 for the LoRA parameter-count illustration. The temperature value 0.33, hardware, prompts and code-access information were already present. These disclosures do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: New Appendix B and Table 4 elaborate the existing positioning against LoFIT, including sparsity control and intervention flexibility. Three learning-rate references—Mnih et al. (2015), Smith (2017) and Smith (2018)—are added. The broader related-work framing remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. v3 makes targeted gate explanations and wording corrections, expands and reorganizes the parameter-comparison discussion and appendices, and adds acknowledgments and affiliation details. This is a localized editorial revision rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn and relocated. The gate-ablation figure becomes Table 2, the model-size table becomes Figure 9, and gate visualizations expand from four to ten heatmaps. v3 also adds Figures 10–11 and comparison tables, splits parameter counts into two columns, and revises plot legends, axes and panel arrangements.

improvement.justification: The additional diagnostics and trainable/active parameter accounting provide useful evidence and clarity. However, v3 Appendix F.3 describes validation-selected baselines while Section 4.3 still describes configuration averaging, despite unchanged benchmark scores. Appendix A also claims input-dependent selection despite Section 3.2 explicitly stating that gates take no input. These newly conflicting descriptions affect central experimental and methodological interpretation, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
